hints: Following rain downhill from every single cell repeats a lot of work. What if you start at the sea and ask which cells could have drained into it?
Reverse flow + DFS from the borders: from each sea's edge cells, walk uphill (to neighbours with height ≥ current). Mark what each sea reaches in its own boolean grid, then take cells marked in both.

1. Make west and east boolean grids.
  2. Flood from every top/left edge cell into west, moving only to neighbours with height ≥ current.
  3. Do the same from every bottom/right edge cell into east.
  4. Collect every cell that is true in both.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: From every cell, run a downhill search and check whether it reaches both seas.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two uphill flood fills from the sea edges, each visiting every cell at most once, then intersect.

explain: For [[1,2,3],[8,9,4],[7,6,5]], the west flood starts on the top row and left column and climbs to everything, since heights rise towards the centre (9). The east flood starts on the bottom row and right column (3,4,5,6,7) and climbs to 8 and 9, but not to 1 or 2 because they are lower than their neighbours. Every cell except (0,0) and (0,1) is in both sets — 7 cells. Note the reversed comparison: water flows down to ≤ heights, so the search moves up to ≥ heights.
recognize: Which cells can reach two different borders by a monotone rule → flood fill backwards from each border and intersect.
